links.comparator_used: Same models forced to always answer (no abstention option), paired same-item analysis on 150 psychiatric MedMCQA items
links.outcome: Paired accuracy when an abstention option was offered vs. forced answering
links.effect: Only the 1.2B model showed a paired effect distinguishable from noise, and it was negative (−6.7 points, 95% CI [−12.7,−0.7]); the 7.6B model's paired effect reversed from a naive +0.8 to −5.3 points (95% CI [−9.3,−1.3]). Naive answered-item accuracy had suggested a modest benefit for three of four models.
links.tradeoff: Self-chosen abstentions were poorly targeted: 8 of the 7.6B model's 12 abstentions forfeited an item it would otherwise have answered correctly. Naive unpaired accuracy on answered items overstated the benefit.
links.quote: We read the surviving evidence as: miscalibration and weak error-detection are general properties of this model family; accuracy ranking is domain-dependent and should not be assumed to transfer; and a prompted abstention option is not a free safety improvement for any of the four models once evaluated with paired, coverage-aware statistics rather than naive answered-item accuracy.
